direction.treatment: A dusk-lit journey from a Mesopotamian city to a Lydian mint to a modern banking screen. The visual throughline is the ledger: clay tablet → coin → digital ledger. Every reconstruction is labelled; maps are simplified.
direction.style: Painterly flat illustration with atmospheric gradients, warm dusk light, layered parallax silhouettes.
direction.typography: Inter Black for titles, Inter ExtraBold captions in the lower third; dates in small caps chips.
direction.camera: Slow parallax push-ins on landscapes; locked-off for diagrams; a single coin-strike punch.
direction.transitions: Cross-dissolves; match-cut from clay tablet to phone ledger at the end.
direction.lighting: Golden-hour key, cool ambient shadows, warm glow on metal.
direction.sfx: Wind and distant market ambience, stylus taps on clay, metallic coin strike, soft UI tick.
direction.safety: Badge 'Artistic reconstruction' on every reconstructed scene; 'Simplified map'; on-screen hedge where evidence is debated.

segments.text: Nearly 4,000 years ago, Mesopotamians lent silver at 20 percent interest.
Yet the first coins wouldn't appear for over a thousand years. So how did money begin?
The classic story says people bartered, a goat for some grain. But no one has ever documented a society that ran on barter alone.
Instead, Mesopotamian scribes recorded debts on clay tablets, measured in silver and barley. A shekel was a weight of silver, about eight grams.
So money may have started as a record of who owed what. Historians still debate the details.
Then, in the late six hundreds BCE, in Lydia, in modern Turkey, people stamped lumps of electrum, a natural gold and silver alloy. The first coins.
Today, the Bank of England estimates most money is bank deposits. Numbers in a ledger, a lot like a clay tablet.

claims.text: Mesopotamian law codes (c. 1800 BCE, Eshnunna and Hammurabi) set interest on silver loans at 20%.
claims.evidence: Mesopotamians made loans of silver or barley at interest rates set by law - under the Ana-Ittisu laws (end of 3rd millennium B.C.), the code of Eshnunna (around 1800 B.C.) and the code of Hammurabi (18th century B.C.) - of 20% for silver and 30% for barley.

claims.text: The earliest coins date to the later 7th century BCE — more than a thousand years after c. 1800 BCE.
claims.evidence: archaeologists from the British Museum discovered ninety-three electrum coins that had been deposited as offerings during the latter part of the seventh century BCE.

claims.text: No pure barter economy has ever been documented ethnographically.
claims.evidence: No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money; all available ethnography suggests that there never has been such a thing.

claims.text: Silver and barley served as units of account and media of exchange in Mesopotamia; one shekel ≈ 8.3 g of silver; loans were recorded on clay tablets.
claims.evidence: since the 3rd millennium B.C., silver and barley ... were used as medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value ... 1 shekel (= 8.3 grams)

claims.text: Money may have originated in credit/accounting rather than as a physical medium; the question is debated.
claims.evidence: barter is usually ill-defined and archaeological evidence about it is inconclusive ... non-monetary transactions have persisted during millennia (R4); any story of how money first developed is mostly based on conjecture and logical inference (R6).

claims.text: The first coins were made of electrum (natural gold-silver alloy) in Lydia (western Turkey) in the later 7th century BCE.
claims.evidence: All earlier coins had been made exclusively of the gold-silver alloy known as electrum ... these earliest coins were inscribed with Lydian names ... minted in Lydia by Lydians. An alloy in which gold occurs naturally

claims.text: In 2014 the Bank of England estimated bank deposits make up about 97% of money in circulation in the UK.
claims.evidence: [bank deposits] make up the vast majority — 97% of the amount currently in circulation.

titles: The Barter Myth: Where Money Really Came From
seo.description:
Long before coins, Mesopotamian scribes recorded debts in silver and barley on clay tablets. The first coins appeared in Lydia in the late 7th century BCE — and today most money is, once again, numbers in a ledger.

Reconstructions are artistic interpretations; maps are simplified. Historians still debate the exact origins of money.
